Learning Objectives
Identify the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors for atypical femur fractures.
Perform an appropriate work up of patients in whom an atypical femur fracture is suspected.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of atypical femur fractures.
Specify the postoperative management of patients with an atypical femur fracture and
osteoporosis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Atypical femur fractures (AFFs) are unusual fragility fractures that occur in the subtrochanteric
and femoral shaft regions.

Table 1 Five Major Features of Atypical Femur Fractures as Described by the Task Force of the
American Society for Bone and Mineral Research
The fracture is associated with minimal or no trauma (such as a fall from standing height or
less).
The fracture line originates at the lateral cortex and is substantially transverse in its
orientation; however, it may become oblique as it progresses medially across the femur.
Complete fractures extend through both cortices and may be associated with a medial spike;


Overview
AFFs were first reported in association with the use of diphosphonates in the early 21st
century. A task force of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research published
an initial consensus statement in 2010 that summarized available case reports and
research and defined atypical fractures.1 A second report was published in 2014, further
refining the diagnostic criteria and recommending management of AFFs.2 The diagnosis
of an AFF requires the fracture to be in the femoral diaphysis from just distal to the
lesser trochanter to just proximal to the supracondylar flare and to meet four of five
major criteria. The five criteria are history of no or minimal trauma, fracture line
originating from the lateral cortex in a primarily transverse orientation, complete
fracture extending across both cortices potentially with a medial spike (Figure1) or an
incomplete fracture of the lateral cortex, noncomminuted or minimally comminuted

(Video 1).

a region of sclerotic cortical bone that meets all five major criteria for an atypical femur

Epidemiology
1.74 AFFs per 10,000 patient-years in women older than 50 years treated with
diphosphonates3
Incidence of AFFs increases with duration of diphosphonate use.3

Epidemiology
In the literature, the precise risk of AFFs varies. The second report from the American
Society for Bone and Mineral Research task force reported the absolute risk of AFF varies
from 3.2 to 50 cases per 100,000 patient-years.2 The largest cohort published included
almost 2 million women and found an incidence of 1.74 fractures per 10,000 patient-
years in women older than 50 years treated with diphosphonates.3 The incidence of
atypical fractures in women not being treated with diphosphonates was 0.10 per 10,000
person-years.3 The rate of atypical fracture increased with the length of time an
individual was taking diphosphonates and subsequently decreased with time since
diphosphonates were discontinued. The incidence of AFFs was higher in patients of
Asian ancestry and in older patients.3 The same cohort demonstrated that after 3 years
of diphosphonate use, 149 hip fractures were prevented for every 2 AFFs in White
women and 91 hip fractures were prevented for every 8 atypical fractures in Asian
women.3
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Pathophysiology is unknown.
Evidence suggests type of stress fracture.


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Although the precise pathogenesis of AFFs is unknown, studies suggest that AFFs are a
type of stress fracture. By affecting normal bone remodeling, diphosphonates may
impair the processes that normally results in healing of stress fractures.2
Risk Factors
Medications: diphosphonates, denosumab, corticosteroids
Ancestry: Asian3,4
Anatomy: varus lower extremity mechanical axis, lateral femoral bowing5
Female sex
Increased weight3

Risk Factors
In addition to diphosphonate use, several risk factors are associated with AFFs. Duration
of diphosphonate use greater than 3 to 5 years is associated with a higher risk of atypical
fracture.3,4,6 Administration of corticosteroids for more than 1 year and denosumab also
are risk factors.3,7 Several studies have reported increased incidence in patients of Asian
descent.3,4 An association also has been found between more varus femorotibial angle,
coxa varus, and lateral femoral bowing and AFFs.5
Prevention
Diphosphonate drug holiday after 3 to 5 years of treatment3
Suspend diphosphonate if patient reports thigh or hip pain.
Prophylactic fixation of contralateral femur


Prevention
Given that the rates of AFFs increase after 3 to 5 years of diphosphonate administration,
each patient should be reevaluated to determine if continued treatment is indicated or if
a drug holiday should be instituted8 (Figure 2). The length of the drug holiday depends
on the type of diphosphonate; the length is 5 years for alendronate, 3 years for
zoledronate, and 1 year for risedronate.9 Studies indicate the risk of AFF decreases by as
much as 70% 1 year after the discontinuation of diphosphonates; however, bone mineral
density also decreases.
Figure 2 Bar graph shows the incidence of atypical femur fractures according to the
duration of bisphosphonate exposure. (Reproduced with permission from Borrelli J Jr,
Lane J, Bukata S, et al: Atypical femur fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2014;28 suppl 1:S36-
S42.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History


Patient History
A thorough patient history and physical examination is the first step in the diagnosis and
management of AFFs. Minor or no trauma is one of the diagnostic criteria for AFFs.
Patients with risk factors for an AFF should be counseled on prodromal symptoms,
especially groin and thigh pain. Of patients diagnosed with an AFF, 34% to 70% report
antecedent groin or thigh pain.10 Approximately 25% of patients who experience an AFF
will have a contralateral AFF (Figure 3); however, this decreases to 18.5% if
diphosphonates are discontinued after the initial fracture.7
Figure 3 Images of a patient with prodromal thigh pain. The patient initially presented
with right prodromal thigh pain. A, AP radiograph of the right hip demonstrates
hypertrophy of the subtrochanteric lateral cortex (circle). B, AP radiograph of the left
knee demonstrates lateral cortical beaking of the mid-shaft of the femur (circle and
arrow). C, AP fluoroscopic image of the right hip shows a fracture through the
hypertrophied cortex (circle), which the patient sustained the next day in her hospital
room as she stood and turned. At a later date, the patient presented with left prodromal
thigh pain. D, AP radiograph of the left knee demonstrates prophylactic nailing, which
the patient elected to undergo given her history. (Reproduced with permission from

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Three stages are seen:
Stage 1: cortical thickening bump (Figure 4)
Stage 2: dreaded black line (a lucent line in the lateral femoral cortex Figure 5)
Stage 3: complete AFF (a subtrochanteric or diaphyseal fracture line originates in the lateral
cortex, extending transversely in orientation; however, it can turn oblique as it progresses
medially)2

fracture. Note the characteristic beaking of the lateral cortex (arrows). (Reproduced from Volgas

Figure 5 Magnified radiograph obtained through the midshaft of the right femur of an 80-year-
old woman with severe osteoporosis demonstrates a subtle periosteal beak with the central
dreaded black line (arrow) and a subtle endosteal beak (arrowhead). (Reproduced with

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is indicated in patients with no radiographic evidence of impending fracture who have
symptoms suggestive of an incomplete AFF.
Incomplete AFF features: focal cortical thickening on the lateral femur on T1-weighted and T2-
weighted images, with adjacent bone marrow edema or inflammation evident on short tau
inversion recovery and T2-weighted images11
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy is indicated if MRI cannot be obtained.


Imaging Studies
A patient who reports thigh or groin pain and is being treated via antiresorptive therapy
should initially undergo radiography of bilateral femurs. On radiographs, an incomplete
AFF will appear as cortical thickening of the lateral femoral cortex or the presence of a
lucent line in the lateral femoral cortex. A complete AFF, by definition, is a
subtrochanteric or diaphyseal fracture line that originates in the lateral femoral cortex
and extends transversely across the femur. If the fracture approaches the medial site, it
may turn oblique. In patients in whom an incomplete AFF is suspected but no
radiographic evidence is present, MRI or bone scintigraphy study may be performed. If
an incomplete AFF is present, MRI will demonstrate focal cortical thickening of the lateral
femur with adjacent bone marrow edema, whereas bone scintigraphy will show
increased uptake and localized periosteal stress reaction in the lateral femoral cortex
(Figure 6).
Figure 6 Images of a patient with right thigh pain. A, AP radiograph of the right hip
obtained after treatment with alendronate for 5 years. B, Coronal T2-wighted fat-
saturated MRI of the right femur shows focal lateral cortical thickening and bone marrow
edema. C, Anterior (left) and posterior (right) full-body bone scans show increased
uptake in the same area of the right femur and more distal in the left femur. (Courtesy of
Anna Greenwood, MD, Richmond, VA.)

Differential Diagnosis
Fragility fracture
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Incomplete AFF
Contraindications
Inability to limit weight bearing
Dreaded black line on radiographs
If a lucent line (dreaded black line) is present on radiographs, 75% of patients will progress to
complete fracture.12
Techniques
Stop antiresorptive medication.
Protect weight bearing.
Check calcium and vitamin D levels and correct as necessary.
Reevaluate regularly.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is reserved for incomplete AFF in patients who are able to limit
weight bearing and present for routine evaluation to monitor for healing and patients
who are not surgical candidates. If nonsurgical management is pursued in a patient with
an incomplete AFF, antiresorptive medications should be discontinued. Patients should
be instructed to protect weight bearing, and calcium and vitamin D levels should be
checked and corrected as necessary.

Surgical Management
Indications
Complete atypical fracture
Incomplete atypical fracture

Indications
Surgical treatment should be pursued in all patients with a complete AFF who are
medically able to undergo surgical treatment. Initial surgical management of incomplete
AFFs also is recommended because patients with an incomplete fracture and a lucent
line have a 75% risk of progressing to a complete fracture.12 Outcomes of patients who
undergo prophylactic fixation have been shown to be superior to outcomes of patients
who progress to a complete fracture.13
Techniques/Procedures
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Long intramedullary fixation
Plate fixation reserved for patients in whom intramedullary fixation is not possible

Surgical Fracture Fixation
The surgical goals in the management of AFFs are the same as those for typical femur
fractures: restoration of length, alignment, and rotation (Video 2). Fixation with the use
of a long intramedullary implant is recommended. Several factors may make fixation of
AFFs more challenging. Femoral bowing must be considered in selecting an
intramedullary implant. Sclerosis at the fracture site may make reaming via standard
techniques impossible. In these patients, the fracture may need to be opened, with the
intramedullary sclerotic area opened with the use of a burr or the sclerotic region
traversed with the use of a sharp awl10 (Figure 7). In periprosthetic fractures or if the

Figure 7 Fluoroscopic image of a hip shows surgical management of an atypical femur
fracture. After malreduction on nail insertion, the fracture is opened, and a sharp awl is
used to take down the intramedullary pedestal. (Reproduced from Githens M, Garner
MR, Firoozabadi R: Surgical management of atypical femur fractures associated with
bisphosphonate therapy. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2018;26[24]:864-871.)
Postoperative Management
Stop antiresorptive medications: diphosphonates and denosumab.
Supplement calcium and vitamin D as necessary.
Consider anabolic therapy with teriparatide or abaloparitide.
Monitor for delayed healing.
Monitor for development of AFF in contralateral femur.

Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, antiresorptive medications, whether diphosphonate or denosumab,
should be discontinued. Discontinuation of diphosphonates reduces the risk of AFF by
70% each year.6 Teriparatide and abaloparitide are anabolic treatment options for some
forms of osteoporosis and have been prescribed to accelerate healing of AFFs.5 The
clinical efficacy of teriparatide/abaloparitide is unproven. The contralateral femur should
be monitored for AFF because at least 20% of patients sustain a contralateral femur
fracture within 2 years postoperatively.15
Complications
Nonunion
Delayed union in 25%
Nonunion requiring revision surgery in 12%15


Complications
Complications associated with fixation of AFFs include potential complications of femoral
fixation for any reason. With AFFs, the rates of delayed union and nonunion have been
reported to be 25% and 12%, respectively15 (Figure 8)
Figure 8 Radiographs of the hip of a 68-year-old woman with a 60-month history of
diphosphonate therapy. A, AP (left) and lateral (right) radiographs demonstrate a right
atypical subtrochanteric femur fracture. B, AP (left) and lateral (right) radiographs
obtained after cephalomedullary nailing demonstrate malalignment. Autogenous bone
grafting was performed 9 months postoperatively because of delayed healing. C, AP (left)
and lateral (right) radiographs obtained 18 months after the initial procedure
demonstrate complete union. (Reproduced with permission from Cho JW, Oh CW, Leung
F, et al: healing of atypical subtrochanteric femur fractures after cephalomedullary
nailing: Which factors predict union? J Orthop Trauma 31[3]:138-145.)
